edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades K–1 (header); footer is only the page number "1"
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades K–1"; footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / POJJA" on every page.

edits.quote: Problem 1: It is your turn. Can you take the last counter on this turn? Circle yes or no under each pile.
edits.fix: Delete. Piles of 1, 2, 3 are answered (yes, yes, no) in seconds and all three reappear as cards in P3; this is the dumbed-down K–1 opener the organizer objects to.

edits.quote: Problem 2: There are 3 counters, and it is your turn. Your partner always plays carefully. Can you be the player who takes the last counter? Circle yes or no.
edits.fix: Delete and let P3 (classify piles 1–12 by playing) open the band; pile 3 is P3's first discovery, so pre-answering it here is a one-minute directed step. Renumber and move P3 onto page 1.

edits.quote: Boxed text at top of page 2: "A pile is a trap when the player whose turn it is will lose if the other player plays carefully."
edits.fix: This is a second rules box in the middle of the activity. Put the trap definition in the opening rules box on page 1 (P3, P7, P8 all use it), or into the text of P3.

k-1.summary: A strong, fully concrete K–1 band: counters are drawn for every task, and the sequence of traps for {1, 2}, a strategy that answers both replies, a flawed game to diagnose (row 3 is the unique error), playing the adult from 9, traps above 12 and 20, the {1, 2, 3} rule change, and two-pile games is all mathematically correct and far from dumbed down. Edits are light: cut the trivial P1 and redundant P2, move the trap definition into the opening rules, and fix the Name/header/footer template.

edits.fix: Delete the Name field from the page template.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades 2–3 (header); footer is only the page number "1"
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades 2–3"; footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / POJJA" on every page.

edits.quote: Find every turn where the player could have taken a different number of counters and then been sure to win.
edits.fix: As worded, turns 2, 3, 4 and 6 all qualify: at turn 4 (pile 10) taking 1 also leaves the losing pile 9, and at turn 6 (pile 3) taking 1 also leaves the losing pile 2, although the moves actually played there already won. The intended answer is turns 2 and 3. Reword: "Find every turn where the player could have been sure to win but made a move that let the other player win."

edits.quote: Is the claim correct?
edits.fix: A child can write "no" and stop. Say what counts as an answer: "Is the claim correct? If not, give a pile where it fails." (5 is such a pile: taking 3 wins, taking 4 loses.)

edits.quote: Is the claim correct?
edits.fix: Same: "Is the claim correct? If not, show a game where copying fails." (The first player takes 1, the copier takes 1, the first player takes 4 from 6, and the copier cannot take 4 from 2.)

grades-2-3.summary: A well-sequenced {1, 3, 4} investigation that starts with play from 6, classifies 1–20 (losing at 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), tests greedy and copying claims, asks for a full plan from 14, extends to 100, contrasts the parity rule {1, 3, 5}, and ends with well-chosen two-pile starts (5/5, 7/2, 6/4 lose for the first player; 6/1, 9/8 win). All diagrams and answers check. The main fix is P5, whose wording also counts turns where the move played was already a winning one; the two claim problems also need to say what an answer looks like.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle · Week 7 · Grades 4–5 (header); footer is only the page number "1"
edits.fix: Header: "Week 7 / Take-away games / Grades 4–5"; footer: "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / POJJA" on every page.

edits.quote: Problem 1: Allowed moves {1, 2}. Describe all the losing piles, and explain why your description is correct for piles of every size.
edits.fix: The band opens with a proof demand, with no play and no recording space. Have children play {1, 2} with counters and label piles 0–14 in a printed strip before describing and explaining, or fold {1, 2} into P2 as the first of two contrasting rules.

edits.quote: Problem 3 (greedy player under {1, 3, 4}) followed by a blank half page
edits.fix: Children must test the greedy player from many starting piles (it wins only from 1, 3, 4, 6, 11). Add a numbered strip 0–20 to mark the piles where greedy wins, keeping the rest of the space for the argument that it never wins above 11.

edits.quote: Find every set of allowed moves that contains 1 and has exactly the same losing piles as {1, 3, 5}.
edits.fix: There are infinitely many such sets (exactly the sets of odd numbers that contain 1), so a child listing sets cannot tell when they are done. Change "Find every set" to "Describe every set".

edits.quote: Problem 5: Allowed moves {1, 2, m} ... For every other m, describe the losing piles. (blank space only)
edits.fix: Finding the pattern for m = 3, 6, 9 (losing piles have remainder 0, 3, ..., m−3 when divided by m+1) requires labelling several rows. Add three or four blank strips 0–20, each with a box to write m.

edits.quote: Find the pile where the repeating starts and the length of the cycle.
edits.fix: The labels repeat with period 5 from pile 10 on (pile 9 is W but 14 is L), but children seeing the cycle L W L W W will likely answer 12. Say "the smallest pile from which the labels repeat".

edits.quote: for every finite set of allowed moves
edits.fix: "Finite set" is beyond the band's vocabulary. Use "for any set of allowed moves, such as {1, 6, 9}".

edits.quote: Mid-page box: "In a game with two piles, a player chooses one pile on each turn ... Give each single pile a value. A pile of 0 has value 0. The value of any other pile is the smallest whole number ..."
edits.fix: This is a second rules box in the middle of the activity. Put the two-pile rule in the problem that first uses it, and put the value definition directly in P8.

edits.quote: Problem 8: Allowed moves {1, 3, 4}. Find the value of each pile from 0 to 20.
edits.fix: Values are defined and computed before anyone has played a two-pile game, so the definition comes before any experience. Insert a problem where children play two-pile {1, 3, 4} games (for example 2 and 2, 7 and 2, 6 and 1, 6 and 4) and decide who wins; this shows that win/lose labels alone cannot decide 6 and 4. Introduce values after that, then keep P8–P10.

grades-4-5.summary: Deep and correct: the greedy player wins only from 1, 3, 4, 6, 11; {1, 3, 5} matches exactly the odd-move sets; {1, 2, m} is a real research-style question; {1, 6, 9} is periodic from 10 with period 5; and the two-pile value problems (6/4 and 12/5 lose; 5/1 and 11/3 win) and the equal-values proof check out, with far more than forty minutes of work. It is the least concrete band: it opens with proofs instead of play, leaves the open investigations (P3, P5) without recording space, and introduces Grundy values by a bare definition in a mid-page box before any two-pile play.

overall.strongest: The K–1 band gives kindergartners and first graders a genuinely full, correct sequence (traps, answering every reply, finding the error, a rule change, two piles) built on drawn counters throughout.
overall.weakest: The grades 4–5 band is mathematically rich but abstract: it starts with proofs rather than play, lacks workspace for its open investigations, and introduces Grundy values by bare definition before children have played two-pile games.
